# Physical retained-cap first variation and conditional secondary response

This is an exact ordinary first-variation theorem, with a mixed
application to the compatible convex-cut erosions already constructed
in `candidate 6748c967393345b9`.
It includes a moving interior mark and the nonsmooth centroid case.
The final section states precisely what a neutral critical cover does
not establish about the actual deepest set.

Throughout d>=1, K is a convex body, y in int K, and

 T_K(y)=max{integral_K f:0<=f<=1, integral_K(x-y)f(x)dx=0}.

Write V=|K|. Its attained hinge representation and unique maximizing
cap are proved in `candidate 49e262af8d182671`:

 T_K(y)=min_u G_0(u),
 G_0(u)=integral_K[1+u.(x-y)]_+dx.                              (1)

Let U be the set of minimizing parameters in (1). It is nonempty and
compact. Off the centroid it is a singleton. At y=g_K it is explicitly

          U={u:1+u.(x-y)>=0 for every x in K}.                  (2)

## 1. Actual erosion hypotheses and the theorem

Let K_e, e>=0, be nested convex bodies with K_0=K. Choose o in int K.
Assume that for all sufficiently small e>0 and one constant C,

        o+(1-Ce)(K-o) subset K_e subset K.                     (3)

At a regular boundary point x of K let n(x) be its outward unit normal,
and write its new radial endpoint as o+(1-t_e(x))(x-o). Suppose

 t_e(x)/e -> v(x)/[n(x).(x-o)]
                  for surface-almost every x in boundary K,  (4)

where v is bounded and measurable. Then v>=0 a.e. All the already
proved compatible convex-cut erosions satisfy (3)--(4), with their
actual contact-maximum physical speed v. Their facets and nonsmooth
boundaries are allowed. In d=1 use the two endpoints and H_0 surface
measure. These are hypotheses about actual bodies, not a formal
independent assignment of facet velocities.

Let y_e=y+e w+o(e), with finite w in R^d. Condition (3) implies
y_e in int K_e for small e. The right derivative exists and equals

 d/de|_(0+) T_(K_e)(y_e)
   =min_(u in U){-integral_(boundary K)[1+u.(x-y)]_+ v(x)dS(x)
                                                -T_K(y)u.w}. (5)

The minimum on the right is attained. In particular, off the centroid,
with the unique optimal hinge u_*,

       T'=-C_T-T u_*.w,
       C_T=integral_(boundary K)[1+u_*.(x-y)]_+v dS.            (6)

The source cap's cutting plane is permitted to pass through a vertex,
edge, or facet. The hinge is a continuous weight and is zero on that
plane, so no closed-boundary facet mass is counted as a fictitious
first-order loss.

## 2. Uniform weighted-shell expansion

Put H(x)=n(x).(x-o)>0 at regular boundary points. It is bounded below
by the radius of an inner ball about o. Radial coordinates give the
shell formula, for a continuous weight f,

 integral_(K\K_e) f(z)dz
  =integral_(boundary K) integral_0^(t_e(x))
       f(o+(1-s)(x-o)) H(x)(1-s)^(d-1) ds dS(x).                (7)

Bound (3) gives 0<=t_e<=Ce uniformly. Thus (4) and dominated
convergence show H t_e/e ->v in L1(dS). On any compact set of hinge
parameters u, the weights

                f_(e,u)(x)=[1+u.(x-y_e)]_+

are uniformly bounded and have a common Lipschitz bound in x. Moving
y_e to y changes every weight by O(e), uniformly in u. Along each
radial shell, replacing its weight by the value at x also changes it
by O(e), uniformly. The total shell has volume O(e), so these errors
are O(e^2), with an additional o(e^2) harmless when y_e has an o(e)
remainder. The factor (1-s)^(d-1) has the same estimate. Consequently

 integral_(K\K_e)[1+u.(x-y_e)]_+dx
  =e integral_(boundary K)[1+u.(x-y)]_+ v(x)dS+o(e),            (8)

uniformly for u in every fixed compact set.

For the fixed-body integral, differentiation with respect to y gives

 grad_y integral_K[1+u.(x-y)]_+dx=-|D_u(y)|u,
 D_u(y)=K intersect {1+u.(x-y)>=0}.                            (9)

This holds for all u. For nonzero u the cutting hyperplane has zero
d-volume, permitting dominated differentiation; at u=0 all integrands
are positive in a neighborhood. The volume |D_u(y)| is continuous in
(u,y), by the same null-hyperplane argument (and by strict positivity
near u=0). Hence (9) is jointly continuous and gives a uniform Taylor
expansion on compact parameter sets. Subtracting (8), we obtain

 G_e(u):=integral_(K_e)[1+u.(x-y_e)]_+dx
        =G_0(u)+e Phi(u)+o(e),                                (10)

uniformly on compact u-sets, where the continuous function Phi is

 Phi(u)=-integral_(boundary K)[1+u.(x-y)]_+v dS
                                      -|D_u(y)|u.w.           (11)

This proof does not require differentiability of a support function,
continuous v, or a smooth cutting section. Even at a supporting facet
where the hinge vanishes, the removed thickness O(e) multiplied by
its hinge height O(e) contributes only O(e^2).

## 3. Compactness of minimizers and the minimum envelope

There is a fixed-radius ball about y_e inside K_e for all small e:
apply (3) to an inner ball about y and absorb the O(e) displacement
of its center. Integrating the positive linear part over this ball
gives G_e(u)>=c||u|| with c>0 independent of e. Also G_e(0)=|K_e|<=V.
Thus every actual minimizing parameter u_e lies in one fixed compact
ball. Each G_e attains its minimum by continuity and coercivity.

Uniform expansion (10) implies that every cluster point of u_e is
in U. For completeness, G_0(u_e)-min G_0 tends to zero because G_e(u_e)
is no larger than G_e at any fixed old minimizer, and the two functions
converge uniformly on the common ball. Compactness then proves the
claim about cluster points. The same coercivity at e=0 proves that U
is compact.

For any u in U, evaluation at u in (10) bounds the upper derivative
of min G_e by Phi(u). Hence its upper limit is at most min_U Phi.
Conversely, along a sequence attaining the lower limit, choose the
actual u_e and pass to a convergent subsequence u_e->u_0 in U. Then

 [min G_e-min G_0]/e
   =[G_0(u_e)-min G_0]/e+Phi(u_e)+o(1)
   >=Phi(u_e)+o(1) ->Phi(u_0)>=min_U Phi.                        (12)

This proves the right derivative and its exact attained minimum.
For every u in U, |D_u(y)|=T_K(y), by uniqueness of the optimal
retained density. Substitution into (11) proves (5).

At a noncentroid the optimal hinge is unique, giving (6). At the
centroid, integral_K[1+u.(x-y)]dx=V, so its positive-part integral
equals V precisely when the affine function is nonnegative on K.
A strictly negative value anywhere on K would, by continuity and
full dimension, be negative on a positive-volume subset. This proves
(2), including boundary parameters. Thus the entire optimizer set,
not just its interior or the parameter zero, is required in (5).

## 4. Exact centroid formula: a gauge penalty for mark drift

Assume y=g_K and write K_0=K-y. Define

 D=integral_(boundary K)v dS,
 B=integral_(boundary K)(x-y)v(x)dS(x).                          (13)

The Minkowski gauge of K_0 is

 p_(K_0)(z)=inf{t>=0:z in t K_0}.

It is finite, nonnegative, and vanishes only at z=0, since zero is
interior and K_0 is bounded. Its polar identity is
p_(K_0)(z)=max_(q in K_0^polar)q.z. This follows directly from
separation of z from the dilates tK_0; K_0^polar is compact.

By (2), U=-K_0^polar. Every optimal hinge is nonnegative on K, so
its boundary cost is D+u.B. Formula (5) therefore becomes

                T'=-D-p_(K_0)(-B-Vw).                          (14)

The actual ordinary centroid has velocity

                        g_(K_e)=y-e B/V+o(e).                 (15)

Indeed (7) applied to the constant and coordinate weights gives
|K_e|=V-eD+o(e) and integral_(K_e)x=Vy-e(Dy+B)+o(e).
Dividing proves (15). Therefore

 T'=-D if and only if w=-B/V,
 T'<-D for every other mark velocity.                           (16)

Following the ordinary centroid to first order is exactly the unique
way to avoid an additional first-order retained-mass loss at an old
centroid. This is a local statement and is not a mixed deepest-point
selector.

## 5. Exact calibrations and status checks

For K=[-1,1], let K_e=[-1+e l,1-e r] with l,r>=0 and y_e=e w.
The physical speeds at the left and right endpoints are l,r, so
D=l+r, B=r-l and V=2. Directly,

 T_(K_e)(y_e)=2-2e max(l-w,r+w),
 T'=-(l+r)-|r-l+2w|.                                         (17)

This is (14), including the tied case and arbitrary drift signs.

For an actual homothety K_e=p+(1-e)(K-p), p in K, and the matching
mark y_e=p+(1-e)(y-p), exact covariance gives T_e=(1-e)^d T.
At a regular boundary point its inward speed is (x-p).n(x)>=0.
Gauss--Green applied to the Lipschitz weight [1+u.(x-y)]_+ gives

 integral_(boundary K)[1+u.(x-y)]_+(x-p).n dS
  =d integral_K[1+u.(x-y)]_+dx+integral_(D_u)u.(x-p)dx
  =T[d+u.(y-p)]                                             (18)

for every minimizing u. With w=p-y, formula (5) gives exactly -dT.
Thus the normalization, motion sign, and nonunique-centroid envelope
agree with actual convex erosions in every dimension.

## 6. A normalized physical secondary-response test

Consider an actual finite compatible mixed family of positive
d-dimensional fibers and one of its already constructed compatible
erosions. Let the physical speed on fiber z be v_z, and write

 M=sum_z |K_z|,   D_mix=sum_z integral_(boundary K_z)v_z dS,
 M_e=M-eD_mix+o(e).

Fix an interior marked point (p,y) and a path (p,y_e) with the expansion
above. Put T=T_(K_p)(y), tau=T/M, and let U_p be its optimal hinge set.
Then the exact derivative of the physical retained-mass ratio is

 d/de|_(0+) [T_(K_(p,e))(y_e)/M_e]
 =1/M min_(u in U_p)
   {tau D_mix-integral_(boundary K_p)[1+u.(x-y)]_+v_p dS
                                                    -T u.w}. (19)

Thus its first-order nondecrease is equivalent to every displayed
hinge row being nonnegative. Off the centroid there is one row. At
the centroid, writing D_p and B_p as in (13), the test is exactly

        tau D_mix-D_p-p_(K_p-y)(-B_p-|K_p|w)>=0.                (20)

If K_p is a polytope, U_p at its centroid is the compact polytope
defined by 1+u.(vertex-y)>=0. Its linear minimum is attained at one
of its finitely many vertices. Hence (19) is an exact finite family
of linear tests whenever the actual v_z and the prescribed w depend
linearly on deformation parameters. No free assignment of v_z is
asserted: it must be the physical speed of a proved compatible family.

For the one-source averaged-field construction, those speeds are
linear in the averaged field, as proved in
`candidate 4c4db2dc9830c76a`.
With mark velocities averaged in the same way, (19) is linear off
the centroid and a minimum of linear responses at the centroid. This
supplies a genuine physical extra test for that finite response problem,
subject to whatever independent conditions select actual mark motion.

## 7. What a neutral critical cover does and does not supply

At an old deepest point selected by maximal T (and then E), the theorem
applies to every prescribed finite-velocity path through that point.
The correct secondary quantity is (19), not an escort derivative or
a count of ordinary cap masses. However, equality of first-order
critical-cover responses establishes neither that this particular
path is deepest for e>0 nor that it remains T-maximal among deepest
points. Membership y_e in the actual fiber follows from (3); deepest
membership is a separate issue.

A minimal exact calibration shows the distinction. In one continuous
dimension take K=[-1,1], K_e=[-1+e,1-e], and y_e=e^2. This is an actual
convex-cut erosion: impose x+e<=1 and -x+e<=1. The two old critical
halfspaces x>=0 and x<=0 cover K_e, each has exactly half its mass,
and their normalized responses are identically neutral. The mark has
w=0, so (14) and (19) give no additional first-order penalty and a
zero normalized T derivative. Nevertheless y_e is not deepest for
any small e>0: its raw depth is 1-e-e^2, strictly below the midpoint's
depth 1-e. Thus first-order neutrality and the correct secondary
first derivative do not certify exact membership in the new deepest
set, even for a smooth-in-parameter actual interval erosion.

For a usable CONDITIONAL branch statement, suppose a separate argument
provides finitely many actual deepest paths Y_j(e) that represent all
maximizers of T on the new deepest set for every small e, each with a
finite velocity. Paths whose old T/M is below the old maximum have
a strict zeroth-order gap and are discarded. Among the tied old paths,
the derivative of the largest retained-mass ratio is the maximum of
the exact derivatives (19). This is the elementary maximum of finitely
many expansions, not an assumption justified by cover neutrality.

Likewise a secondary variational contradiction requires a separately
proved path inside the exact primary extremizer class. Vanishing
primary first derivative alone does not give such a path. Tied first
derivatives in (19) also need not preserve an exact T tie at higher
order; energy-based tertiary selection requires its own actual tie
or branch analysis. No descent of the global mixed objective, no
deepest-center continuation, and no OC conclusion is asserted here.

## 8. Supplementary exact checks

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_physical_retained_cap_first_variation_two_sided.py` passes
2,442 exact checks. It verifies all interval drift branches, constructs
actual axis-facet erosions of a rectangle, clips their moving bodies
by fixed rational halfplanes (including vertex incidences), and uses
each actual cap centroid as the moving mark. The cap areas and first
moments give exact polynomial first derivatives, which agree with
(5). It also verifies the centroid polar-vertex formula and the exact
neutral-cover/nondeepest-mark calibration. The general proof remains
the compact-envelope and weighted-shell argument above.
